problems.notes: Verified against both of LeetCode's own published examples, including the -1 no-eligible-element case. Extends the same BitTrie primitive MaximumXOROfTwoNumbersInAnArray (LC 421) already proved, with an offline MergeSort-by-limit sweep. Benchmark compares a per-query linear scan (O(n*q)) against the offline sorted BitTrie sweep (O((n+q) log(n+q))). Full test suite: 2305 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 1 pre-existing failure in JumpGameVI unrelated to this change (untracked WIP from a concurrent session). Benchmarks project builds clean in Release.

problems.title: Number Of Ways To Reconstruct A Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (map-of-set adjacency, same shape as AccountsMergeTests) + Algorithms/Sorting/MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence for degree ordering. Candidate-parent tree-reconstruction algorithm composed on top: build symmetric adjacency from pairs, sort nodes by degree, for every node but one arbitrary root find its minimal-qualifying-degree neighbor as parent, verify adjacency[node]\{parent} subset-of adjacency[parent], flag ambiguity on a degree tie. Verified against LeetCode's 3 official examples plus a hand-derived two-max-degree-node ambiguity case (all via dotnet test), and cross-checked the benchmark's two independent implementations (BCL Dictionary/LINQ baseline vs. repo HashMap/MergeSort) against each other at both Params sizes via a throwaway smoke harness -- results matched exactly.

problems.title: Swapping Nodes in a Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SinglyLinkedList/SinglyLinkedListNode<T>, fast/slow two-pointer walk (front advanced k-1 steps, then a runner paired with an 'end' pointer so end lands on the kth-from-end node when runner reaches the tail), swapping Values in place -- same node-primitive style as the existing SwapNodesInPairsTests.

problems.title: Minimize Hamming Distance After Swap Operations
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet/DisjointSet (union every allowed-swap pair over index positions, then group indices by root -- same shape as the existing SmallestStringWithSwapsTests) + HashMap<TKey,TValue> as a per-component value-frequency count to compute the minimum achievable Hamming distance for that component.

problems.title: Find Minimum Time to Finish All Jobs
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a monotone virtual DataStructures.Sequence.IRandomAccessSequence of candidate per-worker time limits (same ClosestDivisors/TheKthFactorOfN sqrt-anchoring shape, generalized to a feasibility predicate), each candidate checked via Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.TrySearch reusing PartitionToKEqualSumSubsetsTests' exact k-bucket Choose/Candidates/Unchoose shape with '==' relaxed to '<='.

problems.title: Cat and Mouse II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over a (MouseRow, MouseCol, CatRow, CatCol, Turn) state tuple - the same turn-based optimal-play minimax shape CanIWinTests/PredictTheWinnerTests already use for bitmask/interval DP, here keyed on a 2D grid position tuple instead, with Turn capped at rows*cols*2 (the well-known pigeonhole bound for this problem) standing in for the official 1000-turn rule while keeping the memoized state space finite.
problems.notes: Test expectations for this Hard grid-game problem were hand-derived and manually traced through the implemented recurrence (not transcribed from LeetCode's own example grids, which I could not recall with confidence) - all 3 cases are robust to jump-distance/turn-cap nuances by construction (mouse-wins-immediately-by-reaching-food cases, and a corridor-cornering cat-wins case fully traced by hand).

problems.title: Count Ways to Make Array With Product
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> as a smallest-prime-factor sieve (same Sieve-of-Eratosthenes pattern CountPrimesTests/PrimeArrangementsTests already establish with DynamicArray<bool>, generalized from a composite flag to a factor value) for O(log k) per-query factorization, combined with an exact BigInteger stars-and-bars binomial coefficient (same 'nothing to compose over plain scalars' precedent as SuperPowTests) for the combinatorics.

problems.title: Find Kth Largest XOR Coordinate Value
problems.primitivesUsed: Heap<int, MinHeapOrder<int>> (DataStructures/Heap) as a size-k min-heap over a hand-rolled 2D prefix-XOR pass, exactly mirroring the KthLargestElement (LC 215) precedent; benchmark compares this O(nm log k) approach against a full O(nm log nm) sort-then-index baseline.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning IV
problems.primitivesUsed: Memoizer (Algorithms/DynamicProgramming) driving a (Position, PartitionsLeft) recursion fixed at 3 remaining partitions, with a plain O(n) two-pointer IsPalindrome helper - the exact shape PalindromePartitioningIII already established, just narrowed from a variable k to a fixed 3. Benchmark uses an 'a'*B + 'b' + 'a'*B + 'c' adversarial string (provably no valid 3-way split exists) to force both an unmemoized and a Memoizer-cached version through their full search; verified empirically that memoization overhead dominates at small B but wins decisively (multi-x speedup) as B grows, showing real shared-subproblem savings, not just noise.

problems.title: Closest Subsequence Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: Classic meet-in-the-middle composing three existing primitives: Backtrack.Search (Algorithms/Backtracking, the Subsets precedent) enumerates each half's subset sums, MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (Algorithms/Sorting) orders one half's sums, and BinarySearch.LowerBound over ArraySequence<int> (Algorithms/Searching) locates the other half's closest partner sum - same composition style as ThreeSumClosest/MaximumXORWithAnElementFromArray. Benchmark compares this O(2^(n/2)) approach against a direct O(2^n) all-subsets brute force.

problems.title: Longest Nice Substring
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<char> - divide-and-conquer scan finds the first character missing its opposite-case partner (via Set.Has), splits, recurses on both halves, returns the longer.
problems.notes: Verified against 3 hand-traced cases (mid-string split, whole-string-nice, single-char base case). Benchmark: O(n^3) check-every-substring baseline vs O(n^2)-worst-case Set-based divide-and-conquer, Params(30,150). Full suite 2336 passed / 1 pre-existing skip; benchmark dry-run clean.

problems.title: Form Array by Concatenating Subarrays of Another Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,char> (injective int->char compression, since <=1600 distinct values fit under char's 65536 range) composed with Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.FindAll (KMP) - existing StringMatching primitives only accept ReadOnlySpan<char>, so ints are compressed to chars first, then searched unmodified; each group is matched against the leftmost occurrence in the unconsumed suffix of nums.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 of LeetCode's official examples via hand trace (true case, pattern-never-occurs, overlap-forces-failure). Benchmark: O(n*m) naive per-start rescan baseline vs O(n+m) compression+KMP on a classic KMP-worst-case adversarial input, Params(200,5000); dry run showed the primitive approach pulling ahead (~0.34x ratio) at Length=5000. Full suite 2336 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Car Fleet II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> composed as a monotonic stack of candidate car indices ahead, processed right-to-left (same precedent family as CarFleet/DailyTemperatures/AsteroidCollision) - a candidate is popped for good once proven it can never be the true next-blocking car for the current or any further-behind car.
problems.notes: Verified against both of LeetCode's official examples via full hand trace (matched [1,-1,3,-1] and [2,1,1.5,-1] exactly), plus a same-speed-never-collides edge case. Benchmark: O(n^2) per-car independent forward scan baseline vs O(n)-amortized Stack sweep on a strictly-increasing-speed adversarial input, Params(200,5000); dry run showed the Stack approach pulling ahead (~0.33x ratio) at Length=5000. Full suite 2336 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Number of Restricted Paths From First to Last Node
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra (distances from node n) composed with Algorithms.Folding.Dags.DagFold.Fold (memoized path count from node 1), over a custom IDagTopology witness whose children are neighbors with strictly smaller distance - the restricted-path rule guarantees acyclicity, licensing DagFold over CheckedFold.
problems.notes: Verified by hand trace against LeetCode's own example (n=5, 7 edges) -> 3, matching the official answer, plus a 2-node edge case. Benchmark: NaiveDfs unmemoized recursion vs DagFold-memoized count on a step-1/step-2 graph shaped like FibonacciBenchmarks' recurrence, Params(20,30).

problems.title: Maximum Score of a Good Subarray
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> as a monotonic-increasing stack (DailyTemperatures/CarFleetII precedent), run left-to-right and right-to-left to get each index's nearest strictly-smaller neighbor; answer is best nums[i]*windowWidth among indices whose window contains k.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples via full hand trace (nums=[1,4,3,7,4,5],k=3 -> 15; nums=[5,5,4,5,4,1,1,1],k=0 -> 20, the latter exercising the >= pop condition's duplicate handling). problems.title: Count Pairs With XOR in a Range

Enables the classic O(32)-per-insert/query trie range-count technique: CountLessThan(high+1) - CountLessThan(low).

problems.title: Maximize Number of Nice Divisors
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<int,BigInteger> driving the recurrence maxProduct(remaining)=max(remaining, 2*maxProduct(remaining-2), 3*maxProduct(remaining-3)) - a 'nice divisor' count is the product of the chosen exponents summing to primeFactors (same maximize-product-of-parts shape as Integer Break/LC343), and many different peel-2/peel-3 orders converge on the same remaining budget, which is exactly Memoizer's overlapping-subproblem use case (same idiom as the existing CountAllPossibleRoutes/FibonacciNumber coverage).
problems.notes: 5 xUnit cases pass; all 5 expected values (including 5->6 and 8->18) were derived and cross-checked by hand-tracing the recurrence itself, not solely from memory of LeetCode's official examples. No modular-exponentiation primitive exists in this repo (searched DataStructures/Algorithms - none), so the benchmark deliberately stays within a range (PrimeFactors 40/50, mirroring FibonacciNumberBenchmarks' scale) where a naive un-memoized BigInteger recursion vs. the Memoizer-backed one is a fair, real complexity comparison, rather than reaching for LeetCode's full 1e9 bound (which would need O(log n) modular exponentiation this repo doesn't have - not needed here since the exercise is proving Memoizer suffices, not matching LeetCode's judge limits). Full test suite: 2382 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 0 failed.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Groups Getting Fresh Donuts

Remainder-0 groups are always served first (free); the recurrence searches every serving order of the rest, with many orders converging on the same state.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit cases pass; both expected values (4 for batchSize=3/[1,2,3,4,5,6], 3 for batchSize=4/[1,3,4,6]) were derived by exhaustively hand-enumerating every permutation of the nonzero-remainder groups (not taken from memory of LeetCode's official examples, since one recalled example did not check out under exhaustive verification). problems.title: Merge BSTs to Create Single BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/.../Trees/BinaryTreeNode<TValue> (mutable Left/Right for in-place leaf->subtree splicing) + DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<TKey,TValue> (root-by-value index, removed once spliced in) + DataStructures/Set/Set<TValue> (which values occur as a leaf, to find the one un-merged overall root) + DataStructures/.../Trees/InOrderTraversal + IInOrderHooks (post-splice BST-order validation via a strictly-ascending in-order walk, same composition AllElementsInTwoBinarySearchTreesTests already uses).
problems.notes: 3 hand-verified cases: a successful 2-tree splice, a disconnected forest (no leaf matches any other root -> null), and a splice that succeeds structurally but breaks global BST order (caught by the in-order ascending check -> null). Benchmark compares a linear tree-list scan vs. the HashMap-indexed lookup for finding a leaf's merge target, on a synthetic chain of tiny 2-node trees; each invocation deep-clones the template forest since splicing mutates nodes in place. Verified via the same isolated scratch project described for 1931 (unrelated pre-existing build failure elsewhere in DSAExperimentation.Tests, not caused by this cluster).

problems.title: Maximum Genetic Difference Query
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/.../Trees/BitTrie + BitTrieNode (32-bit max-XOR trie) + DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<BitTrieNode,int> tracking live-value counts per trie node (same technique LeetCodeCoverage/CountPairsWithXorInARangeTests already established), driven by a manual offline DFS over the parent-array tree: insert a node's value on entering it, answer that node's queries with a live-count-aware greedy max-XOR walk, decrement on leaving (BitTrie itself has no Remove, so the count map is what makes 'undo' possible without one).
problems.notes: Both test cases are LeetCode's own published examples for this problem, hand-recomputed here (ancestor path -> XOR -> max) to confirm [2,3,7] and [6,14,7] rather than trusted from memory. Benchmark uses a worst-case chain tree (parents[i]=i-1) so the naive per-query parent-walk baseline pays its full O(depth) cost, contrasted with the O(n+q*32) offline BitTrie DFS. Verified via the same isolated scratch project described for 1931 (unrelated pre-existing build failure elsewhere in DSAExperimentation.Tests, not caused by this cluster).

problems.title: Number of Visible People in a Queue
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> used as a monotonic non-increasing stack of heights swept right to left (same pattern as DailyTemperatures/NextGreaterElementI). No new primitive needed.
problems.notes: Benchmark: O(n^2) definition-literal forward scan vs O(n) monotonic-stack sweep, Params(200,5000), random-permutation heights. Correctness cross-checked with an independent standalone console app (referencing DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks) confirming brute force and stack sweep agree on random inputs and both reproduce the hand-derived classic example [10,6,8,5,11,9] -> [3,1,2,1,1,0]. Full Tests-project build is currently blocked by an unrelated pre-existing compile error in FindTheShortestSuperstringTests.cs (being actively edited by a different concurrent session, not part of this cluster and not touched); the DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks project - which shares the identical algorithm code and the production DSAExperimentation project - built clean with 0 errors.

problems.title: Maximum Compatibility Score Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, closing over tuple state (student, usedMentorMask) - identical (int,int) bitmask-assignment shape to MinimumCostToConnectTwoGroupsOfPointsTests (LC1595), maximizing a per-pair dot-product score instead of minimizing an edge cost. No new primitive needed.
problems.notes: Benchmark: unmemoized bitmask recursion (same asymptotic blowup as trying all m! permutations) vs the Memoizer-routed version, Params(4,7) group size. Correctness cross-checked with an independent standalone console app: brute force and memoized DP agree on random score matrices at GroupSize 3 and 6, and both reproduce the official LeetCode example scores (8 and 0) used in the test file. Full Tests-project build currently blocked by the same unrelated FindTheShortestSuperstringTests.cs issue noted for #1944; DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks (same production dependency, same algorithm code) built clean.

problems.title: Delete Duplicate Folders in System
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - twice over: a Fixtures/FolderNode.cs tree keyed by folder name (composes HashMap the same way TrieNode composes it for chars; added once per project, DSAExperimentation.Tests/.../DeleteDuplicateFoldersInSystem/Fixtures/FolderNode.cs and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/FolderNode.cs, mirroring the existing VisitStateNode per-project-fixture precedent since Benchmarks doesn't reference Tests), and a HashMap<string,int> signature-count map - plus DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over an ArrayIndexedSequence<string> (RemoveSubFoldersFromTheFilesystemTests precedent) to canonically order each node's child signatures before concatenating. No new primitive needed.
problems.notes: Benchmark: O(n^2) pairwise subtree-equality brute force vs the O(n) canonical-signature + HashMap grouping pass, Params(100,1000) top-level duplicate-subtree count. Algorithm rule verified carefully by hand against the official LC1944... (LC1948) example 1 explanation (leaves are excluded from the duplicate-count map entirely - only non-leaf/non-empty-children subtrees are compared - which is what keeps an unrelated leaf like /d/a from being wrongly deleted alongside genuinely duplicated leaves elsewhere), then cross-checked with an independent standalone console app reimplementing the identical algorithm shape (Dictionary/Array.Sort standing in for HashMap/MergeSort) against the official example plus two hand-derived scenarios covering full (not keep-one) deletion of duplicates found at two tree levels simultaneously, and confirming multiple unrelated empty leaf folders are never mistaken for duplicates of one another. Full Tests-project build currently blocked by the same unrelated FindTheShortestSuperstringTests.cs issue noted above; DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks (same production dependency, same algorithm code) built clean with 0 errors.

problems.title: Three Divisors
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + DataStructures.Sequence.IRandomAccessSequence (SquareExceedsSequence witness), the same anchor-at-floor(sqrt) divisor-counting technique FourDivisorsTests/ClosestDivisorsTests already use for LC 1390/1362 - n has exactly 3 divisors iff n is the square of a prime.
problems.notes: Verified via an isolated scratch build (real DSAExperimentation.Tests project currently fails to build for an unrelated pre-existing reason - see overall notes); 4/4 theory cases pass; benchmark's FullRangeScan/BinarySearchAnchored cross-checked to agree on both random inputs and targeted p^2 cases (4,9,25,49,121,169,361 -> true; 100,12,1,2 -> false).

problems.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Substrings
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.Manacher.ComputeOddRadii - read per-center nested radius (not just the longest palindrome), the same move PalindromicSubstringsTests uses for LC 647 - plus plain array prefix/suffix max to build per-split-point best-odd-palindrome-per-side arrays.
problems.notes: Correctness required care: a naive 'mark only each center's maximal reach, then prefix-max' variant (recalled initially) is WRONG - disproved via hand-derived counterexample 'aabaa' (misses nested sub-palindromes like 'aba'). The implemented version marks every nested radius (1..oddRadii[center]), which is provably correct by definition. Verified against both official LC examples (ababbb->9, zaaaxbbby->9) plus a custom nested-palindrome regression (aaaaa->3), and the benchmark's O(n^3) naive-expand baseline vs the Manacher-based approach cross-checked to agree for n in {2,4,6,8,30,90,200,4000}.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Swaps to Make the String Balanced
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> tracking unmatched '[' via Push/TryPop, the same repo Stack ValidParenthesesTests already uses (aliased as RepoCharStack per that file's precedent).
problems.notes: 3/3 theory cases pass (both official LC examples plus the trivial '[]'->0 case). Benchmark's O(n^2) nearest-unmatched backward-scan baseline vs the O(n) Stack-based approach cross-checked to agree for n up to 4000.

problems.title: Find the Longest Valid Obstacle Course at Each Position
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.UpperBound (patience sorting) over DataStructures.Sequence.DynamicArraySequence<int> wrapping DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int>
problems.notes: Per-position longest non-decreasing run: same patience-sorting tails-array approach as the existing LongestIncreasingSubsequenceTests, swapping LowerBound for UpperBound (equal heights extend a run instead of ending it) and recording the insertion index+1 as answer[i] for every element instead of just the final tails length. Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples in an isolated build (9/9 tests passed); DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks project builds clean with the new benchmark included.

problems.title: Minimum Non-Zero Product of the Array Elements
problems.primitivesUsed: None - direct scalar arithmetic (exponentiation by squaring under a modulus)
problems.notes: Formula (2^p-2)^(2^(p-1)-1) * (2^p-1) mod 1e9+7 needs O(log exponent) modular exponentiation, not a data-structure/algorithm composition. No repo container or algorithm primitive applies - confirmed by grepping the repo for Pow/ModPow/Gcd/BigInteger/number-theory helpers (none exist). This is the same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case the repo already accepted as done for SuperPowTests, PowXnTests, and PowerOfTwo (their own comments cite this precedent explicitly), so this follows suit rather than being marked blocked. Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples (p=1->1, p=2->6, p=3->1512) in an isolated build (9/9 tests passed across the cluster).

problems.title: Last Day Where You Can Still Cross
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound (binary search on the answer over IRandomAccessSequence<bool>) + Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (grid connectivity from a virtual node wired to every dry top-row cell)
problems.notes: Crossability is monotone in day, so 'is day d blocked' is the same [false...false,true...true] sequence shape as the existing KokoEatingBananasTests/SplitArrayLargestSumTests; each probe is one DepthFirstSearch.Traverse call (NumberOfIslandsTests' grid-neighbors closure idiom) from a virtual (-1,-1) node connected to every still-dry top-row cell, checking whether the bottom row is reached. Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples in an isolated build (9/9 tests passed); DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks project builds clean with the new benchmark included. Note: DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/FindTheShortestSuperstring/FindTheShortestSuperstringTests.cs currently fails to compile (pre-existing, unrelated to this cluster, appears to be a concurrent session's in-progress edit) - left untouched per git-safety instructions; it blocks a full-solution dotnet build/test until fixed by its owner.

problems.title: Find if Path Exists in Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (Union + IsConnected) directly over the problem's own dense 0..n-1 node ids - no KeyedDisjointSet wrapper needed. Same shape as existing NumberOfOperationsToMakeNetworkConnectedTests/NumberOfProvincesTests. Benchmark: iterative DFS reachability baseline vs DisjointSet, mirroring NumberOfProvincesBenchmarks' DFS-vs-Union-Find contrast.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra (run from the destination) composed with Algorithms.Folding.Dags.DagFold over a custom IDagTopology witness (a neighbor is a child only when it lies exactly on a shortest path: node.Dist - weight == target.Dist) and IFoldAlgebra (sum mod 1e9+7). Same Dijkstra-then-DagFold composition already proven by NumberOfRestrictedPathsFromFirstToLastNodeTests, but with an exact-distance condition instead of that precedent's looser strictly-decreasing one, since this problem counts only true shortest paths (verified by hand against the official n=7 example, expected 4). Benchmark reuses the precedent's Fibonacci-shaped-DAG construction so naive unmemoized recursion is genuinely exponential vs DagFold's memoized version (measured 108ms vs 1.87ms at N=30).

problems.title: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Plain array min/max scan + the private Euclidean Gcd helper this repo already reuses verbatim across CheckIfItIsAGoodArrayTests/XOfAKindInADeckOfCardsTests/NumberOfDifferentSubsequencesGCDsTests (deliberately never promoted to a production primitive per those files' own comments - 'no repo container or algorithm primitive applies here'). Benchmark mirrors CheckIfItIsAGoodArrayBenchmarks' subtraction-vs-Euclidean contrast; widened the value range past LC's literal 1000 bound (to 2,000,000, same departure NumberOfDifferentSubsequencesGCDsBenchmarks/CheckIfItIsAGoodArrayBenchmarks already make) after a dry run showed the O(max) subtraction cost was invisible against the O(n) scan at realistic small values - confirmed subtraction now runs ~2.5x slower than Euclidean.

problems.title: Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,MinHeapOrder<Element>> (this repo's own binary heap) as a size-k min-heap over a problem-local NumericStringToken : IComparable<NumericStringToken> wrapper (compares by digit-string length, then ordinal) - same pattern as the existing KthLargestElementTests (LC215)/KClosestPointsToOriginTests precedents, just with a custom comparable value type instead of int/tuple.
problems.notes: 3 tests pass (classic example, same-length numeric-vs-lexicographic distinction, longer-string-outranks-shorter). Benchmark: Array.Sort+index baseline vs size-k heap; both build and smoke-test correctly via BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry (heap trails FullSort in this cold-start dry run, matching the pre-existing KthLargestBenchmarks.cs's identical qualitative behavior under the same dry-run conditions - not a regression specific to this file).

problems.title: Minimum Number of Work Sessions to Finish the Tasks
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer - bitmask DP over 'which tasks are still unscheduled' (int mask, tasks.Length <= 14), same ParallelCoursesII/SmallestSufficientTeam shape already in this repo, with feasible[mask] precomputed once and submask enumeration (sub = (sub-1) & remaining) picking each candidate session.
problems.notes: 3 tests pass (classic 2-session pack, 5-task 2-session pack, single-session fit). Benchmark: the same recurrence unmemoized (revisits the same mask via different session-split orders) vs Memoizer-cached - dry run confirms correctness and shows the gap widen from 3.3x at TaskCount=6 to 35x at TaskCount=9.

problems.title: Operations on Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (bare successor-function engine, ARCHITECTURE.md section 12) with successors = node => node.Children, used per-query inside Upgrade to collect a node's subtree. Ancestor-lock checks are a plain walk up each node's own Parent field, not a repo primitive - Graph's topology contracts (IGraphTopology/ITreeTopology) are deliberately child-ward only (GetChildren, never GetParent), the same reasoning KthAncestorOfATreeNodeTests' own doc comment already states for that exact gap.
problems.notes: 5 tests pass (full lock/unlock/upgrade sequence matching LeetCode semantics, lock-already-locked, upgrade-self-locked, upgrade-with-locked-ancestor, upgrade-with-no-locked-descendant). Benchmark: naive whole-tree ancestor-chain scan vs DepthFirstSearch.Traverse-based subtree-only scan, repeated over many queries against a leaf node in a large tree - dry run shows the gap grow from 3.7x at NodeCount=2000 to 20x at NodeCount=20000.

problems.title: The Number of Good Subsets
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer - bitmask DP memoized over (candidateIndex, usedPrimeMask) tuple state, same shape as NumberOfWaysToWearDifferentHatsToEachOtherTests. Squarefree-value/prime-mask precomputation is plain test-local glue (int arithmetic), no new primitive.

problems.title: The Number of Weak Characters in the Game
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Attack,int Defense)> with a descending-attack/ascending-defense-tiebreak comparer (tie-break idiom mirrors RussianDollEnvelopesTests), followed by a plain O(n) running-max linear scan.

problems.title: GCD Sort of an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet - values themselves used as dense union-find ids, unioned with their own prime factors via trial division (same PrimeFactors idiom as LargestComponentSizeByCommonFactorTests) - plus Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence<int> for the comparison-sorted copy.

problems.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search<TState,TChoice> (same choose/explore/unchoose subset-enumeration primitive Subsets/SubsetsII already use) enumerates every index-subset of s (LeetCode caps s.Length<=12, so the 2^n subsequence space is the intended solution, not a shortcut); each subset is kept as a (bitmask,length) pair only when it reads as a palindrome, then a plain pairwise scan finds the max length1*length2 over disjoint (mask1&mask2==0) pairs.
problems.notes: Verified all 3 official LeetCode examples ("leetcodecom"->9, "bb"->1, "accbcaxxcxx"->25) both via an independent Python brute-force cross-check and the actual xUnit tests (all pass). Benchmark compares hand-rolled bitmask enumeration (BruteForce) vs. Backtrack.Search-based enumeration (Backtracking) on Length in {8,12}; both build and run cleanly under a BenchmarkDotNet dry job (Backtracking is slower here due to delegate/LINQ overhead at this tiny n - an honest measured result, not tuned to make the primitive win).

problems.title: Smallest Missing Genetic Value in Each Subtree
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse<TNode> (successor-function DFS) composed with DataStructures.Set<int> - only the node holding genetic value 1 and its ancestors can have a non-trivial answer, so DepthFirstSearch.Traverse walks from that node up to the root, at each ancestor step visiting only the newly-reached subtree portion (successors filter out the previously-processed child), folding values into the Set and advancing a running mex counter. Same successor-skip technique already used by MaximumGeneticDifferenceQueryTests (LC 1938) for a different parent-array family-tree problem.
problems.notes: Two hand-derived, hand-verified test cases (a branching tree with value 1 on one branch, and a tree where no node holds value 1) both pass. Benchmark uses a chain-shaped tree (worst case for a naive per-node subtree rescan) comparing BruteForce (O(n^2), fresh HashSet+recursive DFS per node) vs. AncestorChainWithSkip (O(n) total via the composed primitives); a BenchmarkDotNet dry run at NodeCount={200,2000} showed the expected asymptotic crossover - BruteForce ahead at 200 (constant-factor/allocation overhead dominates), AncestorChainWithSkip ~6x faster and ~50x less allocation at 2000.

problems.title: Detect Squares
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> nested inside itself (HashMap<int, HashMap<int,int>>, x -> y -> occurrence count) - the same nested-HashMap composition EvaluateDivisionTests (LC 399) already uses for an unrelated problem's adjacency structure. Count(x,y) only scans points already sharing the query's x-coordinate, deriving each candidate square's other two corners' coordinates directly and checking them via O(1) HashMap lookups.
problems.notes: Verified against the official LeetCode walkthrough example (add (3,10),(11,2),(3,2); count(11,10)=1, count(14,8)=0; add (11,2) again; count(11,10)=2) plus a no-shared-x-coordinate edge case; both pass. Benchmark compares a List-based linear-rescan baseline (ListBased) against the nested-HashMap grouped-by-x approach (HashMapGroupedByX) over a dense point lattice at GridDimension={5,10}; a dry run already showed HashMapGroupedByX ahead (~0.72x time, ~0.17x allocation) at GridDimension=10.

problems.title: The Score of Students Solving Math Expression
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> for interval memoization keyed by (left,right) number-token indices, composed with DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<long,bool> to hold/enumerate each interval's achievable-value set (Set<T> was rejected: it only exposes Has/TryAdd, never enumeration, and combining sibling intervals requires iterating every achieved value).
problems.notes: Different-Ways-to-Add-Parentheses-shaped interval DP. Test uses '2+3*4' (hand-verified: (2+3)*4=20, 2+(3*4)=14 correct) covering the 5/2/0 scoring rule. Benchmark's naive baseline is the same recursion with no caching; a BenchmarkDotNet --job short run confirmed the complexity story (RecursiveNoMemo 265.998us vs MemoizedHashMap 45.700us at NumberCount=10, with memoized 2x slower at NumberCount=6 where constant overhead dominates - the expected crossover). dotnet test: 3/3 passing; both projects build with 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Stone Game IX
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> to bucket stones by value mod 3, feeding the known closed-form parity rule (cnt0 even => cnt1>=1 && cnt2>=1; else |cnt1-cnt2|>=3). Benchmark's naive baseline separately composes Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> for a full negamax game-tree search over (count0,count1,count2,turnSumMod3).
problems.notes: Formula verified by hand against all 3 official LeetCode examples ([2,1]->true, [2]->false, [5,1,2,4,3]->false). Benchmark's game-tree baseline also hand-verified via negamax simulation against the first two examples. BenchmarkDotNet --job short run showed the closed form 53x-139x faster and widening with n (Length=20 ratio 0.02, Length=50 ratio 0.007). dotnet test: 3/3 passing.

problems.title: Smallest K-Length Subsequence With Occurrences of a Letter
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> - the same monotonic-stack-greedy shape as RemoveDuplicateLettersTests, with the pop condition additionally gated on (a) enough characters remaining to reach length k and (b) not dropping the in-stack letter-repetition count below the target.
problems.notes: Algorithm hand-simulated step by step against all 3 official examples (leet/3/e/1->eet, leetcode/4/e/2->ecde, bb/2/b/2->bb) before coding. Benchmark compares an O(n*k) naive window-rescan baseline against the O(n) stack sweep; BenchmarkDotNet --job short run at Length=5000 showed 128.222us vs 20.924us (6.1x), with the gap narrowing as expected at Length=500 (constant-factor-dominated). dotnet test: 3/3 passing.

problems.title: Stock Price Fluctuation
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<int,int> (authoritative price per timestamp) + two Heap<(int Price,int Timestamp),TOrder> instances (MaxHeapOrder/MinHeapOrder) with lazy deletion against the HashMap - the same two-heap composition pattern already used by FindMedianFromDataStreamTests/KthLargestElementInAStreamTests.

problems.title: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference
problems.primitivesUsed: Backtrack.Search (subset-sum enumeration per half, grouped by subset size) + MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence + BinarySearch.LowerBound with a custom IComparer<int> over ArraySequence - the same meet-in-the-middle composition already proven by ClosestSubsequenceSumTests, extended to group sums by chosen-count since both output arrays must be exactly n elements.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Moves to Seat Everyone
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence, applied to both input arrays, then summed index-wise - same composition ArrayPartitionTests already uses.

problems.title: Remove Colored Pieces if Both Neighbors are the Same Color
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Buffers.ContiguousGroupBuffer<TItem,TKey> - groups the string into maximal same-color runs; a run of length L always yields exactly max(L-2,0) removable moves regardless of order, so the game reduces to comparing each player's fixed move budget.
problems.notes: Benchmark: O(n^2) NaiveGameSimulation (actual move-by-move play via List<char>) vs O(n) ContiguousGroupBuffer-based RunLengthCounting. 3 new tests pass; full suite 2538 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Queue.Queue<(int Node,int Steps)> - dual-distance BFS (first and second distinct edge-count depth per node, since every road has equal weight) using the repo's own Queue as the frontier; traffic-signal wait is a plain arithmetic simulation afterward.
problems.notes: Benchmark: ListDequeueBfs (naive List<T> with O(n) RemoveAt(0) dequeue) vs RepoQueueBfs (Deque-backed O(1) Queue<T>) on a single-cycle graph. Verified against both of LeetCode's own worked examples (13 and 11). 2 new tests pass; full suite 2538 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Parallel Courses III
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm) over a CourseTimeNode/CourseTimeTopology IGraphTopology witness (Fixtures/), plus a single forward-relaxation DP pass over the returned order computing each course's earliest completion time - same shape LargestColorValueInADirectedGraphTests already uses.
problems.notes: Benchmark: RepeatedRelaxation (Bellman-Ford-style O(V*E)) vs KahnsTopologicalSortDp (O(V+E)); dry run at NodeCount=1000 showed ~40ms vs ~3.5ms. 3 new tests pass; full suite 2538 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Number of Valid Move Combinations On Chessboard
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search<TState,TChoice> / BacktrackingSteps - the same 'fold pruning into Candidates instead of generate-then-reject' shape BeautifulArrangement/NQueens already use. Candidates enumerates each piece's legal (direction,distance) moves (including staying put) and only offers ones whose simultaneous-movement trajectory never collides, at any shared timestep, with an already-chosen piece; Choose/Unchoose just append/remove from a List<Move>. No new primitive needed - per-piece move enumeration and the timestep collision check are problem-specific glue over Backtrack's existing contract.
problems.notes: Verified against a Python reference brute-force simulation of the exact problem semantics: solo rook@(1,1)=15, solo bishop@(1,1)=8, solo queen@(1,1)=22 (matching known LeetCode single-piece examples), plus two independently-computed 2-piece cases (two rooks at opposite corners=223, rook+bishop at opposite corners=119). Benchmark compares CartesianProductThenValidate (materialize each piece's full candidate list, take the product, validate the whole timeline only once assembled) against PrunedBacktracking (Backtrack.Search); dry-run over [Params(2,4)] pieces executed cleanly with no exceptions on both.

problems.title: Find the Minimum and Maximum Number of Nodes Between Critical Points
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> - representation-only walk over .Next, the same 'just the representation' shape ConvertBinaryNumberInALinkedListToInteger/AddTwoNumbers already use. A running previous value plus first/previous/last critical indices computed in one pass are enough; no algorithm primitive needed beyond the node itself.
problems.notes: Test cases hand-verified against the local-max/local-min rule directly (fewer-than-3-nodes and monotonic-list both -> [-1,-1]; a 7-node zigzag with 3 critical points -> [1,3]; a 9-node list with exactly 2 critical points -> [3,3], min==max). Benchmark compares MaterializeIndicesThenScan (collect critical indices into a List<int>, then a second pass) against SinglePassConstantSpace (folds both passes into one walk, no List<int> allocation), over a strictly sign-alternating zigzag list so nearly every interior node is genuinely critical; dry-run over [Params(200,5000)] executed cleanly with no exceptions.

problems.title: Vowels of All Substrings
problems.primitivesUsed: None - no repo primitive applies, the same 'closed-form single pass over the bare string/array' category this repo's own manifest already established for Gas Station/Candy/Maximum Product Subarray/Ambiguous Coordinates. Each vowel at index i is counted once by every substring containing it - (i+1)*(n-i) - so summing that per-vowel contribution in one O(n) pass is the answer; there is nothing to compose over a data structure.
problems.notes: Test cases use LeetCode's own published examples ('aba'->6, 'abc'->3, 'ltcd'->0), hand-verified against the contribution formula. Benchmark compares SubstringScan (textbook O(n^2) running-count-per-start-index) against ContributionFormula (O(n) closed form); dry-run over [Params(200,5000)] executed cleanly with no exceptions.

problems.title: Walking Robot Simulation II
problems.primitivesUsed: None - O(1) modular-arithmetic index into the fixed perimeter loop (2*(width+height-2)); same 'boundary-shrinking index arithmetic, no repo Representation/Operations primitive to compose' category already established by this repo's Spiral Matrix / Spiral Matrix II / Gas Station coverage.
problems.notes: Verified by hand-simulating step-by-step against the formula at several points (including a full-loop wraparound landing back at the origin facing South) and cross-checking both agree; 3/3 new tests pass. Benchmark compares a naive per-unit-step walker (O(num steps) per Move, mirroring this repo's existing WalkingRobotSimulation LC-874 coverage) against the O(1)-per-move formula; both run cleanly under a BenchmarkDotNet dry job with the expected timing trend as StepsPerMove grows.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Tasks You Can Assign
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over an IRandomAccessSequence<bool> feasibility witness (same 'binary search on the answer' shape KokoEatingBananasTests already uses) + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> as the sliding pool of currently-assignable workers inside the hardest-task-first greedy feasibility check.
problems.notes: Verified against two hand-traced LeetCode examples (tasks=[3,2,1],workers=[0,3,3],pills=1,strength=1 -> 3; tasks=[5,4],workers=[0,0,0],pills=1,strength=5 -> 1) plus a no-pills-infeasible edge case; 3/3 new tests pass. Benchmark compares a linear 'try k=maxK,maxK-1,...' scan against BinarySearch.LowerBound over the same Deque-backed check; at Length=50,000 the binary-search version already runs in ~38% of the linear scan's time under a BenchmarkDotNet dry job, with the gap widening by design as Length grows further (call count O(maxK) vs O(log maxK)).

problems.title: Time Needed to Buy Tickets
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Queue.Queue<(int,int)> - direct line simulation (dequeue, decrement, re-enqueue at the back), the same idiom FindTheWinnerOfTheCircularGameTests already establishes for this Queue<T>.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples via hand simulation (tickets=[2,3,2],k=2 -> 6; tickets=[5,1,1,1],k=0 -> 8); 2/2 new tests pass. Benchmark compares the O(total tickets purchased) Queue simulation against the O(n) closed-form sum; QueueSimulation is ~9-11x slower than ClosedFormSum under a BenchmarkDotNet dry job at both Length=50 and Length=300.

problems.title: Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SinglyLinkedList/SinglyLinkedListNode<T> (internal, InternalsVisibleTo-exposed) - same pointer-splice composition style as the existing ReverseNodesInKGroup coverage, with a variable/truncated group size and reversal keyed on each group's actual (not expected) length parity instead of a fixed k. Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (fetched via web search to avoid a misremembered expected output). Benchmark: plain int[] Array.Reverse baseline vs. the linked-list pointer splice, Params(200, 5000).

problems.title: Process Restricted Friend Requests
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet/DisjointSet (Find/Union/IsConnected) - each request is checked against every restriction via Find alone (comparing current roots) before ever calling Union, so a rejected request never needs an undo/rollback path. Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (fetched via web search; the initially-assumed example 1 output was wrong and corrected before writing the test). Benchmark: from-scratch DFS reachability check per request (FindIfPathExistsInGraphBenchmarks's own DFS-vs-Union-Find precedent) vs. DisjointSet, Params(300, 3000).

problems.title: Range Frequency Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<TKey,TValue> (value -> DynamicArray<int> of ascending indices) + DataStructures/DynamicArray/DynamicArray<T> + DataStructures/Sequence/DynamicArraySequence<T> + Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound (count = UpperBound(right) - LowerBound(left)). Verified against the official LeetCode example (fetched via web search). Benchmark: O(n) brute-force rescan per query vs. the O(log n) HashMap+BinarySearch approach, Params(200, 5000).

problems.title: Find All People With Secret
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.KeyedDisjointSet.KeyedDisjointSet<int> (this repo's composing wrapper around DisjointSet, same primitive AccountsMergeTests already proved out for 'union on shared membership') + DataStructures.Set.Set<int>. Meetings are grouped by timestamp; a fresh KeyedDisjointSet<int> is built per group to union just that group's participants, and Set<int> marks which resulting components touch an already-informed person before a second pass marks the rest of that component informed too. Building a fresh KeyedDisjointSet per timestamp (instead of mutating one global DisjointSet and needing an 'undo union' this repo has no primitive for) is what keeps a same-timestamp-only chain from leaking a false connection into a later timestamp.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (3/3 pass), including the case where a same-timestamp chain must NOT leak connectivity into a later timestamp. Benchmark compares RepeatedRelaxation (an O(k^2)-worst-case per-timestamp fixed-point rescan baseline, forced to pay its multi-pass cost via reverse-ordered chain meetings) against RootMergedWithKeyedDisjointSet; a BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun (real, warmed-up) confirmed the expected crossover: the naive rescan wins at ChainLength=50 (1.09us vs 4.88us) but the primitive-composed approach wins at ChainLength=400 (38.4us vs 65.8us). Caught and fixed a real off-by-one in the benchmark's synthetic person-id budget (IndexOutOfRangeException) via a dry run before the ShortRun. Both Tests and Benchmarks projects build with 0 warnings/0 errors.

problems.title: Finding 3-Digit Even Numbers
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (O(1) expected TryAdd-guards-a-growing-list dedup, the same shape AccountsMergeTests' email dedup uses) + Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (the same 'sort with this repo's MergeSort' convention SortAnArrayTests/AccountsMergeTests already use). A triple nested loop over distinct array positions (not distinct values) builds every valid leading-zero-free, even 3-digit number; Set<int> dedupes; MergeSort produces ascending order.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (3/3 pass), including repeated-digit-at-different-positions dedup and the no-even-digit-available empty-result case. Benchmark compares a List<int>.Contains-linear-scan dedupe + List.Sort baseline against Set<int>-dedupe + MergeSort; a BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun at Length=100 showed the primitive-composed approach ~4.6x faster (1.27ms vs 5.85ms), since the baseline's Contains scan cost grows with the ~450-number result set while Set<int>'s check stays O(1) expected. Both projects build with 0 warnings/0 errors.

problems.title: Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<T> - a slow/fast two-pointer walk over .Next (the same two-pointer shape CycleDetection.cs already uses for Floyd's tortoise-and-hare) finds the middle node's predecessor in one pass, then an O(1) in-place unlink removes it.
problems.notes: Verified against odd-length, even-length, two-node, and single-node (empty-result) cases (4/4 pass). Benchmark compares a two-pass count-then-rebuild-a-new-list baseline against the one-pass in-place slow/fast delete, rebuilding a fresh list from the same source array on every invocation (deletion is destructive) the same way SortAnArrayBenchmarks copies its array fresh per invocation. A BenchmarkDotNet dry run confirmed correct behavior and the expected ~2x allocation reduction (e.g. 1,280,368B baseline vs 640,112B primitive-composed at Length=20000, matching 'build once' vs 'build once + rebuild n-1 extra nodes'). Both projects build with 0 warnings/0 errors.

problems.title: Step-By-Step Directions From a Binary Tree Node to Another
problems.primitivesUsed: LowestCommonAncestor.Find (Algorithms/Ancestry) to locate the turnaround node, then AllRootToLeafPaths.Find (Algorithms/Paths, already used by PathSumII/PathSumIII/KthAncestorOfATreeNode) rooted at that LCA to recover the two root-to-node chains, generic over BinaryTreeNode<int>/BinaryTreeTopology<int>/BinaryTreeChildren<int>/NaturalChildOrder. No new production code.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive find-path baseline against the LowestCommonAncestor+AllRootToLeafPaths composition on a balanced tree (leftmost vs rightmost leaf, so LCA=root, the worst case for AllRootToLeafPaths which collects every leaf path, not just the two needed).

problems.title: Valid Arrangement of Pairs
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (DataStructures/HashMap) keyed by source node, valued by this repo's own Stack<Element> (DataStructures/Stack) of remaining outgoing destinations; Hierholzer's algorithm (DFS consuming one pair per step, appending to the route only at a dead end, then reversing) composed the same way ReconstructItineraryTests already does for LC 332, substituting Stack for Heap since only *a* valid arrangement is required, not the lexicographically smallest.
problems.notes: Start node picked via outdegree-minus-indegree balance (+1 node when one exists, else pairs[0][0] for the Eulerian-circuit case). Hand-verified all three test cases reconstruct exactly LeetCode's own canonical example outputs. Benchmark contrasts Dictionary<int,List<int>> (O(1) tail removal, so the baseline isn't artificially handicapped) against the repo's HashMap+Stack.

problems.title: Detonate the Maximum Bombs
problems.primitivesUsed: DepthFirstSearch.Traverse(start, successors) (Algorithms/Traversal/DepthFirst), the same Func<TNode,IEnumerable<TNode>>-closed reachability walk JumpGameIIITests already composes, with successors computed inline via squared-distance-vs-radius-squared circle-contains-point arithmetic (long-typed, no repo geometry primitive applies to a single-point check, per CircleAndRectangleOverlappingTests' own precedent). Reachable-set size (List.Count) from each candidate start bomb, maxed over all bombs.

problems.title: Sequentially Ordinal Rank Tracker
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> with the existing MinHeapOrder<T>/MaxHeapOrder<T> witnesses (two heaps: a size-pinned max-heap 'topK' + a min-heap 'backup'), keyed on (-score, name) ValueTuples so IComparable<T> already gives the descending-score/ascending-name order. No custom IHeapOrder witness needed.
problems.notes: Verified by hand-tracing all 6 add/get calls of the official LeetCode example sequence before writing the test; matches exactly.

problems.title: Sum of Subarray Ranges
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (indices), used twice for the monotonic-stack sum-of-subarray-maximums/minimums contribution technique - same primitive and pattern already proved out by LargestRectangleInHistogramTests.cs.
problems.notes: Test cases [1,2,3]->4 and [4,-2,-3,4,1]->59 both verified by manual brute-force enumeration of all subarrays before coding.

problems.title: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> (recipe name -> index), DataStructures.Set.Set<T> (supply membership), DataStructures.Queue.Queue<T> (BFS frontier) composed into a hand-rolled Kahn's algorithm pass.
problems.notes: Deliberately does not call Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TrySort: that generic engine requires one uniform IGraphTopology edge relation over every vertex, with no way to express 'some prerequisites are free (supplies) vs. permanently unresolvable (unknown ingredients)' - so a small hand-rolled Kahn's pass (same in-degree/frontier shape) over HashMap/Set/Queue was used instead, not a new production primitive. Also required aliasing DataStructures.Queue.Queue<T> (RecipeFrontier) to avoid a CS0104 collision with System.Collections.Generic.Queue<T> under this repo's ImplicitUsings, matching the existing Stack<T> alias precedent elsewhere in the repo.

problems.title: Check if a Parentheses String Can Be Valid
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Stack/Stack<int> (two instances - unmatched '(' indices and unmatched free/unlocked-position indices), the same two-stack greedy ValidParenthesisStringTests (LC 678) already proved out for '*' wildcards, adapted so locked[i]=='0' plays '*'s role
problems.notes: Verified the two-stack greedy against a brute-force oracle over all 2^k free-position assignments (20k random small cases, 0 mismatches) since LC 2116's free positions can't 'vanish' the way LC 678's '*' can - confirmed the algorithm still holds.

problems.title: Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Connectivity/StronglyConnectedComponents.Tarjan (a size-k SCC is exactly a k-cycle in this out-degree-1 functional graph) + Algorithms/TopologicalSort/TopologicalSort.TrySort (its Kahn-peel 'ordering' out-param lists every off-cycle node in dependency order for free, reused to DP each node's longest incoming chain before its favorite is processed - LargestColorValueInADirectedGraphTests precedent), over a small EmployeeNode/EmployeeTopology IGraphTopology fixture pair under Fixtures/
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (favorite=[2,2,1,2]->3, [1,2,0]->3, [3,0,1,2]->4). Benchmark's hand-rolled ManualPeelAndCycleWalk baseline cross-checked against GraphPrimitiveComposition for NodeCount in {20,200,5000} - identical results.

problems.title: Maximum Twin Sum of a Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SinglyLinkedList/SinglyLinkedListNode<T> to hold the list + DataStructures/Deque/Deque<int> (CircularBuffer-backed) - one forward walk pushes every value to the back, then draining matched front/back pairs together finds each twin sum with no index arithmetic or list reversal
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples ([5,4,2,1]->6, [4,2,2,3]->7). Benchmark's ArrayIndexTwoPointer baseline vs DequeFrontBackDrain cross-checked for Length in {8,200,5000} - identical results.

problems.title: Find Substring With Given Hash Value
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/RollingHash.RollingHash, full-control constructor: custom (power,modulo) RollingHashLane doubled into both lane slots, custom IEqualityComparer<char> encoding val(c)=c-'a'+1, queried over the REVERSED input text so its leftmost-character-gets-highest-power convention reproduces LeetCode's val(s[0])*power^0..val(s[k-1])*power^(k-1) formula.

problems.title: Groups of Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet.DisjointSet over word indices, unioned via a DataStructures/HashMap.HashMap<mask,representativeIndex> that turns each word's 26-bit letter-set mask's add/delete/replace neighbors into O(1) lookups instead of an O(n^2) pairwise scan (AccountsMergeTests/SimilarStringGroupsTests' own union-on-shared-key shape).

problems.title: Design Bitset
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> as the fixed-size raw-bit store, wrapped in a thin Bitset class with a lazy 'flipped' interpretation flag plus a running ones-count for O(1) flip/count/all/one (DesignCircularDequeTests' own 'compose an existing Representation behind a design-problem wrapper' shape).

problems.title: Maximum AND Sum of Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - DP over (Slot, UsedMask) tuple state, same shape MaximumStudentsTakingExamTests' (Row, PrevMask) state already establishes. Each slot independently chooses to stay empty or take 0/1/2 of the still-unused nums elements before advancing to the next slot.
problems.notes: Caught a real correctness bug during dev: the commonly-cited 'slot = popcount(mask)/2+1' simplification (forcing slots to fill strictly in order 1,2,3,...) failed LeetCode's own example 2 (expected 24, got 10) - it's unsound because AND-ing against a later slot index isn't always worse than an earlier one (counterexample added as a test: nums=[3], numSlots=2 must pick slot 2, not slot 1). Fixed with the (Slot, UsedMask) formulation, verified against both official examples plus the adversarial case. Benchmark keeps NumSlots at {2,3} (not {3,5} like MaximumStudentsTakingExamBenchmarks) because this DP's per-slot branching is quadratic in remaining elements (every pair is a candidate), not linear like that precedent's per-row branching. 9/9 new tests pass; both Tests and Benchmarks projects build with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Count Good Triplets in an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> - two Binary Indexed Tree sweeps (forward for left-smaller counts, backward for right-larger counts) over the rank array a[i]=pos2[nums1[i]], the same coordinate-free counting shape CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelfTests/ReversePairsTests already use.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples (answers 1 and 4) plus a too-short-for-a-triplet edge case. Benchmark compares an O(n^2) direct pairwise scan against the O(n log n) double Fenwick sweep, Params(200, 5000) matching CountOfRangeSumBenchmarks/ReversePairsBenchmarks precedent.

problems.title: Merge Nodes in Between Zeros
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> - single dummy-head walk over .Next, same shape AddTwoNumbersTests/RemoveZeroSumConsecutiveNodesFromLinkedListTests already use.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples plus a single-group edge case. Benchmark contrasts a two-pass, intermediate-List<int>-allocating approach against the single primitive-native pass (both O(n) time; MemoryDiagnoser is what separates them), the same 'extra pass vs. single native pass' shape MiddleOfTheLinkedListBenchmarks already establishes for LC 876.

problems.title: Count Array Pairs Divisible by K
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue>: nums[i]*nums[j] % k == 0 depends only on Gcd(nums[i],k) and Gcd(nums[j],k), so every index is grouped by its own gcd via HashMap<int,int>, then only pairs of the (k-divisor-bounded) distinct group keys are checked - O(n + d^2) instead of O(n^2). Gcd is a private Euclidean-algorithm helper, the same inline pattern FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayTests/GCDSortOfAnArrayTests already use (not a new production primitive).
problems.notes: 4 new tests pass. Benchmark compares this against O(n^2) brute force; dry run confirmed correctness and a genuine crossover (primitive ~3.7x faster at Length=5000, though brute force wins at Length=200 due to HashMap/gcd constant overhead - an honest result, same spirit as ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks tolerating FloydWarshall losing).

problems.title: Counting Words With a Given Prefix
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Trie.Trie<TValue>: the exact Insert+HasPrefix pairing CheckIfAWordOccursAsAPrefixOfAnyWordInASentenceTests (LC 1455) already uses - one word inserted alone per candidate, then HasPrefix(pref), counting matches instead of returning the first index.
problems.notes: 4 new tests pass. Benchmark mirrors CheckIfAWordOccursAsAPrefixOfAnyWordInASentenceBenchmarks' shape (StartsWithScan baseline vs. per-word Trie<bool>).

problems.title: All Ancestors of a Node in a Directed Acyclic Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm, exact CourseScheduleII/LoudAndRich precedent) composed with DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,bool> as each node's ancestor set (chosen over Set<Element> because Set doesn't expose enumeration of its contents, which the propagation needs). Nodes ordered source-to-sink; each node's own already-finalized ancestor set plus itself is unioned onto every child in one linear DP pass.
problems.notes: New Fixtures/AncestorNode.cs + Fixtures/AncestorTopology.cs (IGraphTopology witness), same shape as CourseSchedule/LoudAndRich fixtures. 3 new tests pass, hand-verified against LeetCode's own n=8 worked example. Benchmark compares a naive one-DFS-per-start-node forward walk (LoudAndRichBenchmarks' shape) against the TopologicalSort+HashMap DP pass on a capped-fan-out DAG; both run correctly in a dry-run smoke test.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Moves to Make Palindrome
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<char> (Sorting's IIndexedSequence<Element> Get/Set contract) driving the standard greedy two-pointer adjacent-swap palindrome algorithm; benchmark compares that representation against a BCL List<char> RemoveAt/Insert implementation of the identical O(n^2) algorithm (ARCHITECTURE.md SS8's 'performance independence' case).
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts (classic even-length case, odd-length case needing a middle-character nudge, already-a-palindrome edge case), all hand-verified by simulation and passing. Build+test run clean (7/7 across the cluster). Benchmark dry-run executes without exceptions on Length in {200, 2000}.

problems.title: Replace Non-Coprime Numbers in Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<long> (DailyTemperatures/NextGreaterElement precedent) holding the merged prefix, with a file-local Gcd/Lcm helper (same inline-helper precedent as FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayTests) driving the cascading-merge-while-non-coprime loop.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts (both hand-verified against my own from-scratch simulation of the stack algorithm, matching the well-known editorial results for these inputs), passing. Benchmark contrasts an O(n) amortized Stack<long> cascade against an O(n^2)-ish repeated-full-rescan List<long> baseline; dry-run shows the expected asymptotic win at Length=2000 (8.8ms vs 1.2ms).

problems.title: Minimum Weighted Subgraph With the Required Paths
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra/AStar over the existing WeightedNode/WeightedTopology/ListEdges<TNode,TWeight> edge-topology fixtures (NetworkDelayTime precedent for the test; WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology Benchmarks-project fixtures for the benchmark) - run once forward from src1, once forward from src2, and once on a locally-built edge-reversed graph from dest, then min-summed per candidate meeting node.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts (a hand-computed 5-node graph verified independently by both the dist-sum formula and by tracing the actual union-of-edges subgraph to the same total, plus an unreachable-dest case), passing. Benchmark contrasts per-node point-to-point AStar queries against the single-Dijkstra-per-source-plus-reverse-graph approach; dry-run confirms the expected large win (23ms -> 3.9ms, ~100x less allocation at NodeCount=150).

problems.title: Longest Substring of One Repeating Character
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> keyed by index, with a test-local RunSegment/RunAggregate custom ICombineOperation<RunSegment> witness implementing the standard run-length merge (prefix/suffix/max run length, bridging when the left child's rightmost char equals the right child's leftmost char) - the same open-extension pattern NumberOfLongestIncreasingSubsequenceTests' LisAggregate already establishes for this interface. Update O(log n); Query(0,n-1) O(1) via the tree's full-cover fast path.

problems.title: Find Triangular Sum of an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<Element> - each Pascal's-triangle-style reduction round is built as a fresh DynamicArray<int> via Add/Get/Count. No faster (sub-O(n^2)) algorithm is composable from existing primitives - confirmed via grep that this repo has no modular-binomial-coefficient/Lucas'-theorem machinery - so the benchmark compares a raw int[] baseline against the DynamicArray-based version of the identical O(n^2) simulation to isolate the primitive's overhead.

problems.title: Sum of Scores of Built Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.ZFunction.Compute over the reversed input string - score(t_i) (LCP of s's length-i suffix with s itself) is exactly the Z-value at position i of reverse(s); summed for i=1..n-1 plus n for the whole string. Verified against both official LeetCode examples (expected sums 9 and 14) by hand-deriving the Z-array before writing the tests. O(n) vs. the O(n^2) brute-force baseline benchmarked alongside it.

problems.title: Encrypt and Decrypt Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - one HashMap<char,string> for the keys[i]->values[i] encryption mapping, one HashMap<string,int> as a precomputed frequency table over every dictionary word's encryption, turning decrypt into an O(1) average lookup instead of re-encrypting the whole dictionary per call.
problems.notes: Verified against the official example (Encryptor(['a','b','c','d'], ["ei","zf","ei","am"], dictionary).encrypt("abcd")=="eizfeiam", decrypt("eizfeiam")==2). Benchmark compares RecomputeEveryDecrypt (re-encrypt the whole dictionary per decrypt call) vs PrecomputedFrequencyMap; dry run showed the gap widen from 1.7x at DictionarySize=50 to 9x at DictionarySize=2000, with allocation dropping from 50MB to 725KB. 8/8 new tests pass; both Tests and Benchmarks projects build with 0 errors/warnings.

problems.title: Maximum Total Beauty of the Gardens
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort (sort ascending) + DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound (used twice: as a below-height element counter over the sorted ArraySequence<int>, and as a monotone true/false search over an implicit IRandomAccessSequence<bool> feasibility sequence for the tallest affordable height) - the same 'search-on-the-answer' idiom KokoEatingBananasTests and ClosestSubsequenceSumTests already establish in this repo.
problems.notes: Verified by hand against both official LeetCode examples (flowers=[1,3,1,1],newFlowers=7,target=6,full=12,partial=1 -> 14; flowers=[2,4,5,3],newFlowers=10,target=5,full=2,partial=6 -> 30) before coding, then confirmed by the passing test. My own added edge-case test (all gardens already >= target, newFlowers=0) caught a real correctness bug in the classic split-enumeration algorithm: when the array's global minimum is already >= target, the height-search's cost-below-h formula stays 0 all the way to the target-1 cap (nothing ever needs raising), fabricating a phantom achieved height and inflating beauty far past the true max (406 instead of the correct 9 in that case). Fixed with a guard (only add the partial-credit term when sorted[0] < target) proven correct by case analysis: the fictitious inflation only occurs when the count-below-height at the resolved h stays 0 throughout the tested range, which happens iff sorted[0] >= target - genuine incompleteness (sorted[0] < target) always makes the formula converge at the true, non-fictitious minimum instead. Benchmark (LinearSearchOnAnswer vs SortAndBinarySearch) needed its budget tightened (a generous newFlowers let the linear descent from the height cap succeed on its first probe, hiding the O(target) worst case) and target scaled with Length; after the fix, dry run showed a genuine complexity gap (0.65x ratio at Length=200 growing to 0.01x - i.e. binary search ~100x faster - at Length=2000). 8/8 new tests pass (3 for this problem); both projects build with 0 errors/warnings.

problems.title: Design an ATM Machine
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - HashMap<int,long> keyed by banknote denomination holding each denomination's count, the same 'category counters in a HashMap instead of separate fields' shape DesignParkingSystemTests already establishes.
problems.notes: Verified against the official example sequence (deposit([0,0,1,2,1]); withdraw(600)==[0,0,1,0,1]; deposit([0,1,0,1,1]); withdraw(600)==[-1] with state unchanged; withdraw(550)==[0,1,0,0,1]). Added a second test proving the algorithm is strictly greedy (not a general coin-change search): withdrawing 60 from a state holding only $20s and $50s fails ([-1]) even though three $20s would work, because the greedy walk takes one $50 first and 10 has no smaller-denomination cover; a follow-up withdraw(20) confirms the failed call left state untouched. Benchmark (FiveFieldDispatch vs HashMapDispatch) dry run showed HashMap consistently losing to raw array indexing (3x-5.7x slower) as expected for a fixed 5-key space with real hashing overhead - comment corrected to honestly reflect this ('expected to lose', ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks' FloydWarshall framing) rather than an initial wrong guess that it would show no overhead. 8/8 new tests pass (3 for this problem); both projects build with 0 errors/warnings.

problems.title: Longest Path With Different Adjacent Characters
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold + DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Folding.IFoldAlgebra + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering.ListChildren/ITreeTopology - a general n-ary tree built from parent[] (CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's own RoomNode/RoomTopology shape, mirrored here as test-local PathNode/PathTopology fixtures) folded bottom-up via a new problem-specific LongestPathAlgebra: DiameterAlgebra's 'two tallest child heights' composition generalized with a per-edge validity check (a child only contributes to the through-node path when its label differs from its parent's, carried on a PathState that - unlike HeightDiameterState - also threads each node's own label upward so Combine can compare it against every child). No new production primitive: TreeFold/IFoldAlgebra/ListChildren/ITreeTopology are all pre-existing engines; only the algebra and node/topology fixtures are new, in the same Fixtures/ subfolder + duplicated Benchmarks/Fixtures/ copy pattern RoomWaysAlgebra already establishes.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts, hand-verified by simulating the algebra by hand (root-with-two-valid-children -> 3 nodes; two-branches-under-root -> 3 nodes; single node -> 1) since these are node-count answers rather than edge-count diameters. Benchmark compares a naive per-node baseline (mirrors DiameterOfBinaryTreeBenchmarks' RecomputedHeightPerNode: a fresh, unmemoized Height() walk plus a separate recursive best-path search at every node, O(n) x n = O(n^2) on a skewed chain) against TreeFold+LongestPathAlgebra's single O(n) pass, on an alternating-label skewed chain (worst case for the naive baseline, matching DiameterOfBinaryTreeBenchmarks' own Setup rationale). Dry-run smoke test confirmed both benchmark methods execute and cross over as expected: at NodeCount=200 the fold is ~2x slower (constant-factor generic/closure overhead dominates), but at NodeCount=2000 the naive baseline balloons to ~31.5ms while the fold stays at ~2.0ms (~15x faster), demonstrating the intended O(n) vs O(n^2) split. Both Tests (Debug) and Benchmarks (Release) projects build with 0 warnings/0 errors; all 3 new tests pass.

problems.title: Count Lattice Points Inside a Circle
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Set.Set<Element> (HashMap<Element,bool>-backed) keyed by a (int X, int Y) tuple - each circle's own bounding box is scanned for integer points inside it (dx*dx+dy*dy<=r*r), and TryAdd de-duplicates the union across overlapping circles the same 'membership is the whole job' way TwoSumTests already uses HashMap<int,int> for a different key type.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts, both hand-verified: a single unit circle at (2,2) gives the classic 5-point plus shape, and two overlapping unit circles at (0,0) and (1,0) each cover 5 points sharing exactly (0,0) and (1,0), so the correct de-duplicated union is 8 (not the naive 10) - this specifically proves Set's dedup is load-bearing, not just present. Benchmark compares a full-combined-bounding-box scan checking every point against every circle (O(totalArea * circleCount)) against the per-circle-bounding-box + Set approach (O(sum of each circle's own area)); dry-run smoke test confirmed both run correctly and the Set-based approach wins by 1.3x-4.5x as circle count grows (circles scattered across a bound much wider than their radius, so the combined box is far larger than the sum of local boxes). Both projects build with 0 warnings/0 errors; both new tests pass.

problems.title: Count Number of Rectangles Containing Each Point
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> (grouping rectangle lengths by height) + DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort (sorting each height's length bucket and the distinct-height list, via ArrayIndexedSequence<int>) + DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound (over ArraySequence<int>, applied twice per query: once to skip to the smallest height >= y, then per surviving height bucket to skip to the smallest length >= x, whose count-from-there is Length - index) - the same LowerBound-over-a-sorted-ArraySequence composition QueriesOnNumberOfPointsInsideACircleTests already establishes, nested one level deeper.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts using both of LC 2250's own published examples, hand-verified by simulation (rectangles=[[1,2],[2,3],[2,5]], points=[[2,1],[1,4]] -> [2,1]; rectangles=[[1,1],[2,2],[3,3]], points=[[1,3],[1,1]] -> [1,3]). Benchmark compares brute-force O(n*m) direct rectangle-vs-point checks against the grouped+sorted+binary-search approach; dry-run smoke test confirmed both execute correctly and showed a genuine crossover - the grouped approach's fixed setup cost (building the HashMap, MergeSort-ing every bucket) makes it slower than brute force at RectangleCount=500 (~4.9x), but it wins at RectangleCount=4_000 (~0.6x, i.e. ~1.7x faster) once (n+m)log(n) undercuts n*m by more than that setup cost - the benchmark's doc comment states this honestly rather than claiming unconditional superiority. Both projects build with 0 warnings/0 errors; both new tests pass.

problems.title: Sum of Total Strength of Wizards

problems.title: Booking Concert Tickets in Groups
problems.primitivesUsed: SegmentTree<int,MaxOperation<int>> + SegmentTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (DataStructures/SegmentTree) over per-row available-seat counts; BinarySearch.LowerBound (Algorithms/Searching) via a local IRandomAccessSequence<bool> adapter (HasCapacitySequence) reusing the repo's existing 'binary search on the answer' idiom (prefix max over a growing window is monotonic) to find the leftmost qualifying row for Gather in O(log^2 n); Sum tree answers Scatter's feasibility check in one range query.
problems.notes: No new production primitive needed. Verified against the official LC example sequence (gather(4,0)->[0,0], gather(2,0)->[], scatter(5,1)->true, scatter(5,1)->false) plus two edge-case tests. Benchmark compares a raw-array O(n)-per-call baseline vs. the segment-tree+binary-search approach over a fixed random operation stream (RangeSumQueryMutableBenchmarks' fresh-rebuild-per-run precedent); at RowCount 200/2000 with 300 ops the array scan actually wins on raw wall-clock (segment-tree constant factors not yet amortized at this scale), which is an expected, honest result, not a bug - all 3 tests pass and both benchmark methods run correctly under BenchmarkDotNet.

problems.title: Steps to Make Array Non-decreasing
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<(int Value, int Step)> as a monotonic (non-increasing) stack tracking each pending value's own removal step - directly mirrors the existing DailyTemperaturesTests/DailyTemperaturesBenchmarks monotonic-stack pattern, generalized from 'wait days' to 'removal step'.
problems.notes: No new production primitive needed. 3 tests pass (LC example ->3, already-sorted ->0, strictly-decreasing ->1). Benchmark compares an O(n)-per-round brute-force simulation baseline vs. the O(n) monotonic-stack sweep over a fixed random array (RepoIntStack/RepoStack alias convention matched); a --job short run confirms the monotonic-stack version allocates ~20x-115x less memory than the round-simulation baseline, as expected.

problems.title: Minimum Obstacle Removal to Reach Corner
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra (Heap<T,TOrder>-backed) over a small Fixtures pair (ObstacleGridNode + ObstacleGridTopology : IEdgeTopology<...,ListEdges<...>,int>) modeling the grid as a 0/1-weighted graph - edge weight is the target cell's own obstacle flag (0 empty, 1 obstacle), mirroring DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks.Fixtures.WeightedGridNode's shape (each project owns its own copy since Tests/Benchmarks don't reference each other's internal types).
